Diagnostic tests are utilized for various purposes, including diagnosis, aiding in diagnosis, screening, monitoring, assessing predisposition, prognosis, prediction, and determining physiological status. 2. Intimate partner violence refers to behaviors by one individual in a close relationship that cause physical, psychological, or sexual harm to the other. This includes physical violence, sexual violence, emotional or psychological abuse, and controlling behaviors. 3. Key populations are specific groups at higher risk of HIV due to particular behaviors, regardless of the epidemic type or local context. These groups include men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons or other closed settings, sex workers, and transgender individuals. 4. A lay provider is someone trained to deliver healthcare-related services but lacks formal professional or para-professional certification or tertiary education. 5. Multi-analyte testing involves using the same platform to test for different analytes with distinct reagents, often requiring multiple specimens. This is similar to multiplex testing, which tests a single specimen for multiple analytes using one device, such as detecting HIV-1/2 antibodies and syphilis antibodies simultaneously. 6. Negative predictive value refers to the likelihood that a person with a negative test result is truly not infected with HIV. 7. A non-reactive test result indicates no reaction suggesting the presence of an analyte, such as HIV-1 p24 antigen or HIV-1/2 antibodies. 8. Nucleic acid testing (also known as molecular technology, such as PCR or NASBA) detects very small amounts of viral nucleic acids (RNA, DNA, or TNA) both qualitatively and quantitatively. 9. With the client’s consent, these partners are offered HIV testing services (HTS) through provider-assisted or patient referral approaches. 10. 11. A policy is an institutional statement guiding actions within a specific domain. 12. Positive predictive value refers to the likelihood that a person with a positive test result is truly infected with HIV. 13. Pre-test information is a concise discussion providing accurate details to a client, often delivered by a lay provider or health worker before an HIV test. 14. Provider-assisted delayed referral (or contract referral) occurs when an HIV-positive client agrees to disclose their status to partners and suggest HIV testing within a set timeframe. If the partners do not access testing within this period, the provider contacts them directly to offer voluntary HIV testing. 15. The provider then offers voluntary HIV testing to these partners, contacting them via phone, email, or in-person and providing home-based or facility-based testing options. 16. The provider then offers voluntary HIV testing to the partners. 17. 18. Quality control (QC) verifies that a product meets quality standards, identifying and rejecting defective products. 19. Quality improvement (QI) involves proposing solutions to enhance quality and reliability, increasing user satisfaction. The plan/do/check/act cycle is often used in this process. 20. A quality management system directs and controls an organization’s efforts to meet quality objectives through systematic and process-oriented approaches. 21. A rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is an in vitro diagnostic device using immunochromatographic or immunofiltration methods to detect HIV-1/2 antibodies and/or HIV p24 antigen. 22. A reactive test result indicates the presence of an analyte, such as HIV-1 p24 antigen or HIV-1/2 antibodies. 23. Repeat testing involves additional testing during the same visit using the same assay and specimen due to inconclusive or discrepant HIV test results. 24. Retesting involves testing a second specimen from the same individual using the same testing algorithm as a quality assurance step, performed at a later time. 25. Sensitivity refers to the probability that an HIV assay or algorithm correctly identifies all specimens containing HIV-1/2 antibodies and/or HIV-1 p24 antigen. 26. Analytical sensitivity is the smallest amount of analyte (antibodies or antigen) an assay can accurately detect, including different subtypes like HIV-1 group O. 27. Diagnostic sensitivity is the percentage of HIV-infected individuals correctly identified as HIV-positive by an assay or testing algorithm. 28. Seroconversion sensitivity is an assay’s ability to detect HIV infection as antibodies evolve from IgM to IgG during seroconversion. 29. Sentinel surveillance is conducted at selected sites among specific populations to approximate prevalence in a larger population, such as antenatal clinics. 30. Seroconversion occurs when an individual’s immune system produces detectable levels of HIV-1/2 antibodies. 31. A serodiscordant couple consists of one HIV-positive partner and one HIV-negative partner. 32. A serology assay detects antibodies in human specimens, typically using serum or plasma but also whole blood or oral fluid. Examples include rapid diagnostic tests, immunoassays, and supplemental assays. 33. Social network-based HIV testing extends partner services by encouraging individuals with HIV or at ongoing risk to invite members of their sexual, drug-injecting, or social networks to participate in voluntary HIV testing services. 34. Specificity refers to the probability that an assay or algorithm correctly identifies specimens without HIV-1/2 antibodies and/or HIV-1 p24 antigen. 35. Analytical specificity is an assay’s ability to distinguish the relevant analyte from others, minimizing false reactivity, including cross-reactivity. 36. Diagnostic specificity is the percentage of HIV-uninfected individuals correctly identified as HIV-negative by an assay or testing algorithm. 37. A strategic plan translates policy into planned activities with strategic objectives, typically valid for one year in relation to a budget cycle. 38. Supplemental testing involves additional assays to gather more information and ascertain HIV status. 39. Task sharing redistributes tasks between healthcare providers with varying levels of training, such as trained lay providers. 40. Testing for triage involves a trained provider conducting a single HIV RDT and referring individuals with reactive results to a health facility for confirmatory testing. 41. A testing algorithm specifies the products used in a testing strategy, including product name, code, manufacturing site, and regulatory version. Algorithms may change based on verified product combinations. 42. A testing strategy is a sequence of tests conducted to achieve specific objectives, such as infection screening or diagnosis. 43. Throughput refers to the number of specimens tested per hour per operator or the volume of clients served in a facility, laboratory, or community setting. 44. Unassisted HIV self-testing involves individuals using a self-test kit with manufacturer-provided instructions. Users may also access additional support, such as hotlines or instructional videos. 45. Verification confirms, through objective evidence, that specified requirements have been fulfilled.
